analysis.one_liner: Bans the use of hydrofluoric acid at petroleum refineries to prevent mass-casualty releases.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban hydrofluoric acid at roughly 40 oil refineries, introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors in December 2024, died in committee without a hearing or vote when the congressional term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to ban the use of hydrofluoric acid (hydrogen fluoride) in petroleum refining — immediately for new refineries and within five years for existing ones, with no waivers and a $37,500 civil penalty per violation. About 40 U.S. refineries use the chemical to make high-octane gasoline, and a large release could kill or permanently injure thousands of people within 25 miles. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 14 million people living in communities around the refineries that use hydrofluoric acid, including many communities already carrying disproportionate environmental burdens, plus refinery workers who would be exposed first in any release. If the bill passed, they would face a far lower risk of a mass-casualty accident, disaster, or attack releasing a toxic cloud that could kill or permanently injure thousands within a 25-mile radius.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits hydrofluoric acid at any new refinery immediately, and at all existing refineries starting five years after enactment, with no waiver the EPA could grant to let a refinery keep using it.
Removes a hazard that Congress's findings say puts more than 14 million people at risk of death or permanent injury from a single large release, which could reach up to 25 miles from a refinery.
Backs the ban with a $37,500 civil penalty per violation, making continued use of the chemical a costly, enforceable offense rather than a suggestion.
Relies on refining methods already commercially proven and used by the majority of U.S. refineries, so the bill extends existing practice rather than demanding an unproven technology.

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum refiners that use hydrofluoric acid would bear the cost of converting roughly 40 refineries to alternative high-octane refining methods within five years, including permitting and equipment replacement; some portion of those costs would likely reach consumers through gasoline prices, though the bill text does not estimate them.

drawbacks.text: A flat five-year deadline for converting all existing refineries is a short runway for permitting and installing new alkylation units, and the bill allows the EPA no waiver authority even where a refinery shows genuine hardship.

The conversion would be expensive for the roughly 40 refineries still using hydrofluoric acid, and some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through gasoline prices; the bill includes no cost estimates or assistance.

The leading alternatives, such as sulfuric acid alkylation, are safer on-site but carry their own hazards, including the road transport of large volumes of sulfuric acid, so the swap reduces one catastrophic risk while not eliminating alklyation hazards entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large but statistical: it targets a low-frequency, high-consequence catastrophe — a toxic cloud that could kill or permanently injure thousands within 25 miles of about 40 refineries — where Congress's own findings say safe, commercially proven replacements already exist and are used by most U.S. refineries. The costs are real but concentrated: refiners would fund retrofits within five years, with no waiver flexibility and no cost assistance, and consumers might see some of that at the pump. On balance the bill trades a manageable, spread-out compliance cost for eliminating one of the largest mass-casualty chemical risks in the country, though a longer timeline or waiver provision would have softened the burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee two weeks before the term ended and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, so it died when the 118th Congress adjourned in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters introduced the bill on December 16, 2024, joined by 10 Democratic cosponsors, all from the bill's original roster of sponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the only committee action it ever received.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote. The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies operating the roughly 40 refineries that use hydrofluoric acid are better off, because they avoid a federal mandate and conversion deadline. Residents living near those refineries are left with the same risk the bill was written to remove.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 16, 2024, to ban hydrofluoric acid at petroleum refineries.

for.name: Reps. Lieu, Barragán, Cohen, Ramirez, Garcia, Norton, Tlaib, Kamlager-Dove, Scanlon, and Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a small all-Democratic base of support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 16, 2024, and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that never scheduled the bill for consideration during the final two weeks of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Petroleum refining industry
against.role: Operators of refineries using hydrofluoric acid alkylation
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have long resisted mandatory phase-outs of hydrofluoric acid alkylation in federal chemical-safety proceedings, citing conversion costs.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all 11 members attached to the bill were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: About 40 U.S. refineries would have five years to convert to alternative high-octane refining methods or stop using the chemical, facing $37,500 penalties per violation. Their compliance cost is the flip side of the public's safety gain.

Companies that build and install the safer, commercially proven alkylation systems used by the majority of U.S. refineries would win a new retrofit market across roughly 40 refineries. Their gain runs alongside the public's interest in removing the hazard.
